sections.label: What Google wants from local content in 2027
paragraphs: All right, if you own a home service company and you count on Google to bring in calls for you, this video is absolutely for you. Google spent 2026 spelling out what kind of pages it wants, and it's moving booking and calling right into its own search results. Its AI answers reach a ton of people as well. Google said in June that AI Overviews have over two and a half billion monthly active users, and AI Mode has now passed 1 billion monthly active users.

So today we are going to go over what Google wants for local content in 2027 and what we do about it here at ASP. We'll cover what Google wants on your pages, the longer questions homeowners are asking, city pages, bookings from Google, and how to measure all of it. So let's get right into the first one.

sections.label: Part 1: Non-commodity content
paragraphs: All right, so what we're going to talk about first is what does Google mean by non-commodity content? Commodity content is kind of the generic stuff that anyone could write, the same five business tips that you see on every website. But non-commodity content is just the opposite, because it's built on real experience and goes beyond the common knowledge. Now, Google's example of commodity content is a post called 7 Tips for First-Time Homebuyers.

And Google says that kind of post typically adds very little unique insight. And I think we've all probably read like a hundred of those anyway. So now think about your website. Let's say a post called 5 Signs Your AC Needs Repair. That could just sit on just about any HVAC website in the country without ever having to change a word of it. But now picture your lead tech explaining what they check first when a homeowner calls and says, hey, my AC is running but the house won't cool down.

A page built on that answer could only come from your company, and in my opinion that's the kind of page that Google is describing. So what I want you to do this week is pull up your top service page and read it like a competitor wrote it. And if it would still be true on their website, it needs something that only your team knows.

sections.label: Part 2: Effort and originality
paragraphs: All right, number two is effort and originality. Google's page on creating helpful content, last updated October 5th, lays out what its search raters look at when they judge a page. Search raters are people who essentially grade page quality for Google, and two of those really stand out for local businesses. Effort is basically how much real human work went into the page, and originality is whether you're saying something that isn't already on a ton of other websites.

So Google also says that pumping out a lot of text with AI without anyone overseeing counts as little to no effort. Now, Google doesn't ban AI. It actually says that fact check and review anything AI writes before you publish it. And I cannot express that enough. You have to absolutely have a human in the loop.

But Google also says the raters don't control rankings. So I wouldn't treat this like a ranking checklist we think of. It is still the clearest picture that Google gives of the page it wants you to build. And in our view, the part of the competitor can't copy is the text and stuff that office staff already knows, so they're answering questions all day long from your customers. You need to build content that's just like that.

Our approach, what we like to do is we like to have short recorded conversations with the owner, or maybe a lead technician, maybe an office staff, and we'll ask something like, hey, what's the question customers ask you most about a water heater call, or an HVAC replacement or repair?

And then we build the page around that answer using their words. So if you want an action item for this week, sit down with your best technician, write down three questions that they hear the most, and that's a really easy place to start for website content.

sections.label: Part 3: Longer questions
paragraphs: All right, number three is longer questions. Google said in May in the US, the average AI Mode search is three times as long as a traditional search. So think about what that looks like for you and your company. A homeowner used to type, you know, furnace repair or furnace repair near me. They may now ask something along the lines of about what noise their furnace is making at night.

Why is it making it? How old is this furnace? Uploading a picture, using Google Lens, like there's a ton of things now that homeowners are doing to try to help troubleshoot and gain more information about what's going on, versus just trying to find someone who knows what they're looking at. But questions like that will show you what homeowners are actually worried about, and your page can answer those worries before they even pick up the phone.

The tempting move is to build a brand new page for every one of those questions. Google says don't do that. Building separate pages of every version of the question, mainly to just game rankings or AI answers, breaks its spam rules. Google also says a pile of pages doesn't make your website any higher quality. Google's AI can run a bunch of related searches at the same time to answer a question like that.

So in our view, our opinion, one service page that covers the whole job has more chances to match those searches than a page built on just one specific phrase, if you have to pick between the two. So start with the questions your office hears on the phone and the ones your techs hear in the driveways of the house that they're working on. And if a question fits a service you do, answer it right on that service page and in your words, you know, the customers use.

sections.label: Part 4: City pages and the swap test
paragraphs: All right, number four is going to be the swap test. If you haven't heard of it, I'm going to go through this with you. In our experience, city pages are where a lot of homeowners' websites cut corners. Spam rules from Google talk about something called doorway abuse, which is pages that get made just to rank for a bunch of similar searches. And one of the examples Google gives is pages aimed at different cities or regions that funnel people to one specific page.

Now, it doesn't mean every city page breaks the rules. A city page with real local substance helps the person who lands on it, and that's the kind of page that you want to build. So recently Google ran one of its big ranking updates, called a core update, back in March of 2026. After that, a local marketing agency wrote that if the site had 15 or 20 locations pages that all roughly looked the same with just the city name swapped, those pages lost rankings.

Now, that's one specific agency's read, not controlled data. So take that for what you will. What I would do is I would run what's called a swap test. First, if you swap in different towns name and read the page again, if the sentence is still true, nothing on that page specific to the town it's for. And swap in a competitor's name and read it again. If it's still true, nothing on that page is specific to your company either.

So slapping a new city name on a page that fails isn't going to fix it. What it needs is stuff that only is true in that specific town, like neighborhoods, landmarks in that area, photos taken in and around it — needs real jobs your team is done there, without giving, obviously, any customer personal data. But if you want, pause this video right now, go try it for yourself.

What we really like to do is we like to structure the overall design of the page for locations pages. And then we have obviously our service copy of things that we're targeting for that service in that location. And then we have AI help us put together some very specific details about that city. Again, it can be neighborhoods, it can be, you know, depending on your business, right? If you're in landscaping, be soil types, common things that people run into. It could be depths of sprinkler lines.

So you know that like, hey, if you're digging past, you know, X amount of inches or feet, like you need to contact the city phone number to help them come out and show you where all the lines are at. Like all of those things could be unique content that gets put on those pages to help get past this, you know, the spam ranking rule.

sections.label: Part 5: Booking and calling in local results
paragraphs: All right. So number five is booking and calling. And a lot of it is moving into local results. There's even things we're seeing now that there's direct links to book home services in those local results. Now, they usually go through like an Angi Thumbtack or something like that, but it is available in the U.S. and it is happening now. So if you already use software or CRMs like that to run jobs and scheduling, make sure you reach out to that company and ask whether your account can show up in AI Mode if you're not already seeing it.

Now, on the flip side, other companies are also reporting that Google's testing removed links like call buttons from the map listings of local businesses inside the AI Overviews. We didn't find a Google announcement specifically of that test, but I just keep, rather, keep an eye on it and see what's going to be changing over the next couple of months. I think more homeowners in 2027 are going to look, are going to book a call from Google without really ever opening your website.

It's an expectation that we're seeing. It's a trend that we're seeing. There's no specific measurement that Google has said that. It's just something that we're kind of keeping an eye on, that trend. So for you as a business owner, keeping your Google Business Profile accurate, make it easy for homeowners to book and call from your website, and track where every call and booking comes from, because that's how you know what is working.

sections.label: Part 6: Measuring local content
paragraphs: All right, number six, measuring local content. Google gave owners some new ways to measure search content this year, which I think is really cool. Search Console, which, if you don't have a Search Console account, you definitely need to get that set up, get that connected. It's a free tool from Google that shows you how your site does in search, and it also now reports on AI features, and Google says they've rolled it out to all websites.

So everyone has access to these features now. Those reports show how often your pages from your site showed up in things like AI Overviews and AI Mode. Now, when you're in there checking the settings that include your site and Google AI features, because Google says your site has to be included there to be eligible to show up. So make sure you go and do that. The other thing I'd set up is linking between Google Analytics and your Google Business Profile.

It was earlier this year that you were able to connect the two, and you'll see your Business Profile numbers like calls, bookings, and website clicks. This is really huge. I think this is something that everyone drastically undermines. You need to have these tools to look at your data, to make marketing decisions, to be able to see your results and how you're ranking.

Because the booked jobs are the ones that pays bills, right? We judge content by the calls and booked jobs it brings in, and we measure it at a cost per booked job. So if clicks from the regular Google search results hold steady, but your Business Profile calls drop, we need to check the Google's results page and what it shows for your search before we start rewriting content.

And sometimes the page itself isn't necessarily the problem. The other piece is timing. Google released its November core update on the 10th of November this year. Google recommends waiting at least a full week after the update is finished before starting to compare the numbers to see kind of how everything plays out.

So I hold off judging any of your pages by the November update until probably the first week of December has gone all the way through. And then you go back and look and then check year over year as well for that week of December to see where you're at with your organic rankings.

sections.label: Where to start before the end of 2026
paragraphs: So just a quick recap. If you only have time for a few things before the end of 2026, this is where I would start. First, check that you have your Search Console set up. Make sure your site's included in the AI features and see which pages show up. Then make sure your Google Analytics and your Google Business Profile are linked so you can see the calls and bookings right next to your website data.

The second thing is rewrite your top three pages with real conversation from your lead technicians and your office staff. Run the swap test. Take a look at all the locations pages. See if they hold up. Keep your Business Profile accurate and make it easy to book a call from your website. Once Google posts that the November update is done, again, wait a week before you judge how it hits your site.

Compare that week before it started and then also compare the year over year. None of this comes with a guarantee. Nobody outside Google controls what results it shows.
